title: Positive behaviour support
blurb: Explain what positive behaviour support aims to do and build a behaviour support plan with proactive, preventive and reactive strategies.
question: Sam, 23, has a severe learning disability and lives in supported living. He throws objects most afternoons when the house gets busy. The team asks the nurse to lead a positive behaviour support plan. What should the plan contain, and in what order of priority?

teach.body: Positive behaviour support (PBS) is a values-led, person-centred framework for understanding behaviour that challenges. It is based on assessing the social and physical context in which behaviour happens, and it uses that understanding to build support that improves quality of life for the person and those around them. In plain English: understand why the behaviour happens, change what is around the person and teach new skills, so the person's life gets better and the behaviour is needed less.
teach.cite: Gore et al. (2013), definition of PBS

teach.h: What NICE says the aim is
teach.body: NICE NG11 says support should aim to improve quality of life and prevent, reduce or stop future episodes of behaviour that challenges, delivered in the least restrictive setting, with the focus on improving the person's support and increasing their skills rather than changing the person. A behaviour support plan should be developed as soon as possible, based on a shared understanding of the function of the behaviour.

teach.h: Layers of a behaviour support plan

levels.label: Primary: meet needs, change environment, teach skills

teach.caption: Most of the plan, and most of staff time, sits in primary prevention.

teach.h: What goes in each part (NICE NG11 1.6.1)
head: Part
Examples
rows: Teach an alternative skill for the same need
How to respond if risk of harm escalates
teach.caption: The plan also covers risk management, training needs, who delivers it and a named coordinator.
Some services use colour bands so all staff recognise the stage and respond the same way.

teach.body: If a behaviour gets the person something they need, such as a break from noise, the plan teaches another way to get the same thing: a 'break' card, a sign, or a word. NICE NG11 calls this developing an alternative behaviour that achieves the same purpose through a new skill, such as improved communication or emotional regulation. Staff must then honour the new request every time, or the old behaviour returns.

items.label: if restrictive practices rise or quality of life falls

teach.caption: NICE NG11 1.6.1: plans are monitored with continuous objective data.

teach.body: Sam, 23, throws objects most afternoons when housemates return and the house gets loud. The functional assessment suggests escape from noise. Proactive: a quiet lounge, headphones, and a walk at 4 pm. Skill: a 'break' card he hands to staff. Preventive: when Sam paces and covers his ears, staff offer his card and walk. Reactive: move others away, give space, no physical intervention unless serious harm is imminent. Reviewed fortnightly with data.

teach.text: PBS is not a set of consequences, rewards for compliance or a restraint protocol with a friendly name. A plan made mostly of reactive strategies, or one aiming to 'stop the behaviour' without improving quality of life, is not PBS.

items: PBS: values-led, person-centred, based on understanding the behaviour's context and function.
Main aim: better quality of life; behaviour reduces as needs are met.
Primary prevention (meet needs, change environment, teach skills) is the largest part.
Secondary prevention responds to early signs; reactive strategies are a last resort.
NG11: review fortnightly for 2 months, then monthly; named coordinator.

summary: You can now explain the aims and values of positive behaviour support and build a behaviour support plan with proactive, preventive and reactive parts in the right balance. You can teach a functionally equivalent skill and keep the plan under review as NICE NG11 recommends.

A.q: A new support worker asks what the primary aim of positive behaviour support is. Which answer is best?
options: To stop behaviour that challenges as quickly as possible
To improve the person's quality of life
To make the person follow house rules
To reduce the need for staff on each shift
A.why: PBS is a values-led framework whose central aim is improved quality of life; reduction in behaviour that challenges follows from meeting needs.

whyNot.0: Rapid suppression of behaviour is not the aim and can mean restrictive practice.
whyNot.2: Compliance is not the purpose of PBS.
whyNot.3: Staffing levels are not the purpose of PBS.

A.q: Which strategy in a behaviour support plan is an example of primary prevention?
options: Offering a walk when the person starts to pace
Moving other people away during an incident
Reducing noise in the lounge in the afternoons
Recording the incident on an ABC chart afterwards
A.why: Primary prevention changes the environment and meets needs before any signs of distress. Reducing noise removes a known trigger.

whyNot.0: Responding to pacing is secondary prevention: early signs.
whyNot.1: Moving people away during an incident is reactive.
whyNot.3: Recording is data collection, not a prevention strategy.

A.q: How often does NICE NG11 recommend that a new behaviour support plan is reviewed during its first two months?
options: Weekly
Monthly
Every 3 months
Fortnightly
A.why: NG11 1.6.1: review frequently, fortnightly for the first 2 months and monthly thereafter, sooner if restrictive interventions increase or quality of life falls.

whyNot.0: Weekly is more often than the guideline states.
whyNot.1: Monthly is the frequency after the first 2 months.
whyNot.2: Every 3 months is too infrequent for a new plan.

B.q: Jo, 30, has a learning disability and hits her head when asked to do tasks she finds hard. The functional assessment shows the function is escape from demands. Which skill-teaching strategy best fits PBS?
options: Teach Jo to sign 'help' or 'break' and honour it
Remove all tasks from Jo's day to prevent incidents
Insist that Jo completes each task before a break
Give Jo a reward each day she does not hit her head
B.why: PBS teaches a functionally equivalent alternative: a way to ask for help or a break that achieves the same purpose, which staff then honour.

whyNot.1: Removing all tasks reduces her opportunities and quality of life.
whyNot.2: Insisting on completion increases the demand that triggers the behaviour.
whyNot.3: Rewarding absence of behaviour does not teach a new way to meet the need.

B.q: A behaviour support plan for Kai, 26, lists twelve reactive strategies and two proactive ones. What is the main concern?
options: The plan needs more physical interventions listed
The plan should be signed by a psychiatrist
The plan is weighted towards reacting, not preventing
The plan should be reviewed every three months
B.why: In PBS most effort sits in primary prevention. A plan dominated by reactive strategies is unlikely to improve quality of life or reduce the behaviour.

whyNot.0: More physical interventions would make the plan more restrictive.
whyNot.1: Sign-off is not the issue; the balance of strategies is.
whyNot.3: NICE suggests more frequent review, and the balance is the main concern.

B.q: Sara, 35, starts to pace and cover her ears, which her plan lists as early warning signs. Which response matches secondary prevention?
options: Hold her hands to stop her covering her ears
Offer her headphones and a quiet room
Tell her that pacing is not allowed indoors
Call for extra staff to prepare for restraint
B.why: Secondary prevention responds to early signs with calming and diverting strategies, such as reducing sensory input and offering a quiet space.

whyNot.0: Holding her hands is a restrictive intervention and may escalate distress.
whyNot.2: A verbal rule does not address the need behind the early signs.
whyNot.3: Preparing for restraint skips de-escalation and the plan's early strategies.

C.q: Sam, 23, throws objects most afternoons when the house gets noisy. His new 'break' card works for a week, then the throwing returns. Staff say they are 'too busy' to respond to the card in the afternoon. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Withdraw the card because it has not worked
Add a reactive strategy for when he throws objects
Request antipsychotic medication for the afternoons
Review staffing so the card is honoured every time
C.why: A functionally equivalent skill only replaces the behaviour if it works reliably. The plan must make sure staff can respond; NICE expects plans to fit the resources of those delivering them.

whyNot.0: The card worked when honoured; the problem is implementation.
whyNot.1: Adding reactive strategies does not fix the cause of the relapse.
whyNot.2: NICE NG11 1.8.2 considers antipsychotics only if other interventions have not produced change, treated coexisting problems have not helped, or risk is very severe; a plan that staff are not delivering is none of these.

C.q: A care home wants to introduce PBS for Ollie, 40, whose behaviour has increased since his day centre closed. Which first step best fits NICE NG11?
options: Write a behaviour support plan from staff observations
Develop a shared understanding of the function of his behaviour
Introduce a reward chart for days without incidents
Arrange a sensory room session every afternoon
C.why: NG11 says the behaviour support plan should be based on a shared understanding of the function of the behaviour, so assessment and formulation come first.

whyNot.0: A plan without functional understanding may target the wrong need.
whyNot.2: Reward charts do not address why the behaviour started.
whyNot.3: NG11 1.7.7 says not to offer sensory interventions before a functional assessment of the sensory profile.

C.q: Six weeks into Leah's behaviour support plan, the data show fewer incidents but staff have locked the kitchen to prevent food throwing. Leah, 29, now spends more time in her room. What should the nurse conclude?
options: The plan is working because incidents have fallen
The plan should be closed because the aim is met
The plan needs review: restriction is up and life quality down
The plan should add more restrictions to keep progress
C.why: NG11 says plans should be reviewed if restrictive interventions increase or quality of life decreases. Fewer incidents at the cost of restriction is not PBS success.

whyNot.0: Incident numbers alone do not show success if quality of life falls.
whyNot.1: The aim of PBS is a better life, which is not met here.
whyNot.3: More restriction moves further from PBS values.

reteach.title: Fix the world, not the person
reteach.question: If a smoke alarm keeps going off, do you remove the battery or find the source of smoke?

blocks.body: Behaviour that challenges is like an alarm: it tells you a need is not being met. PBS finds the source (noise, boredom, pain, demands), changes the surroundings, and teaches a better way to ask. Reactive strategies are the fire extinguisher: necessary sometimes, but not the plan.

blocks.text: Fewer incidents with more locked doors is not success. Check quality of life alongside the behaviour data.

explain.body: PBS is person-centred and values-led, aiming for a better quality of life, with less behaviour that challenges as a result.

test.q: Which outcome best shows that a PBS plan is succeeding?
options: More PRN medicine is being used
Staff report fewer incidents each week
The person does more things they enjoy
The person stays in their room more
test.why: PBS measures success by improved quality of life, such as more enjoyable, meaningful activity.

whyNot.0: More PRN use suggests more restriction.
whyNot.1: Incident counts do not show quality of life.

explain.body: Meet needs, change the environment, structure enjoyable activity, teach new skills. The largest part of the plan.

test.q: Which is a primary prevention strategy?
options: A visual timetable for the day
Calling for help during an incident
Offering distraction when agitated
A debrief after an incident
test.why: A visual timetable increases predictability before any distress occurs.

whyNot.2: Distraction at early signs is secondary prevention.

explain.body: Secondary: respond to early warning signs with calm and diversion. Reactive: keep people safe, least restrictive, as a last resort.

test.q: Which statement about reactive strategies in PBS is correct?
options: They are the core of a good plan
They are a last resort within the plan
They replace proactive strategies
They should be used at early signs
test.why: NICE NG11 1.9.1: reactive strategies are a last resort, used together with proactive interventions.

whyNot.2: Reactive strategies are used alongside proactive ones.
whyNot.3: Early signs call for secondary, calming strategies.

explain.body: NG11 1.6.1: fortnightly for 2 months, then monthly, sooner if restrictive interventions rise or quality of life falls. A named coordinator.

test.q: A plan started three months ago. How often should it now be reviewed as a minimum under NICE NG11?
options: Every week
Every fortnight
Every 6 months
Every month
test.why: After the first 2 months, NG11 recommends monthly review.

whyNot.0: Weekly is not the stated minimum.
whyNot.1: Fortnightly applies to the first 2 months.
